items.title: LangChain ecosystem
items.takeaway: LangChain is a Python framework that adds functionality around LLMs. It's split into core, chains/agents, LangGraph, LangSmith and LangServe, and its `Document` is just page content plus a free-form metadata dict.

items.title: LangGraph basics
items.takeaway: LangGraph builds an app as a graph: a typed shared State flows through Nodes (functions), ToolNodes run tools, and a StateGraph compiles it all into a Runnable.

items.title: Prompt templates and output parsers
items.takeaway: Chat prompt templates inject the user's variables into a reusable message structure, and output parsers turn the model's text back into clean strings, dicts or validated Pydantic objects.

items.title: RAG from scratch in LangChain
items.takeaway: The "RAG from scratch" map has six stages: query construction, query translation, routing, retrieval, indexing and generation. The basic build counts tokens with tiktoken, embeds with OpenAI (1536 dims), compares by cosine, and retrieves k nearby chunks.

items.title: BPE tokenizer
items.takeaway: Byte Pair Encoding learns its vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens, which compresses text into shorter token sequences.

items.title: Cosine vs L2 similarity
items.takeaway: For semantic embeddings, meaning lives in the vector's direction, so cosine similarity beats Euclidean distance. Once vectors are normalised, a plain dot product is the cosine.

items.title: Encoder vs decoder models
items.takeaway: Encoders see the whole input in both directions and are built to understand. Decoders see only the past and are built to generate, which is why LLMs are decoders.

items.title: LLM embeddings and pooling
items.takeaway: A token starts as a row in the embedding matrix, gains context as it passes through the transformer layers, and pooling collapses the per-token states into one sentence embedding.

items.title: Self-attention
items.takeaway: Attention lets every token directly look at every other token's representation, whatever the distance, which fixes the long-range dependency problem of RNNs at an O(n²) cost.

items.title: Subword tokenization
items.takeaway: Subword tokenization keeps common words whole and breaks rare words into meaningful pieces, which avoids both the huge vocabulary of word-level tokens and the long sequences of character-level ones.

items.title: Context window and KV cache
items.takeaway: The context window is a hard token limit per forward pass, and the KV cache stops the model recomputing keys and values for tokens it has already processed.

items.title: Decoding strategies
items.takeaway: Greedy always takes the top token, sampling (top-k or top-p) adds controlled randomness, and beam search tracks several candidates. Top-p adapts best, and beam search is a poor fit for chat.

items.title: Hallucination
items.takeaway: A hallucination is fluent, confident output that isn't grounded in any source. That's different from a factual error the model learned from bad training data.

items.title: Logits and temperature
items.takeaway: Temperature divides the logits before softmax: below 1 the distribution sharpens, above 1 it flattens, and at 0 it becomes greedy decoding.

items.title: Prompt engineering
items.takeaway: Prompt engineering is structuring, designing and refining the input instructions so the model gives accurate results. A good prompt has a format, a system prompt, context, constraints and an output structure.

items.title: LLM training pipeline
items.takeaway: Pre-training on raw text gives a base model that only continues text, and alignment (SFT, then RLHF or DPO) teaches it to follow instructions and behave.

items.title: LoRA and QLoRA
items.takeaway: LoRA fine-tunes a model by freezing its weights and training two small low-rank matrices, and QLoRA adds 4-bit quantization of the frozen weights to save even more memory.

items.title: Decomposition vs IR-CoT
items.takeaway: Decomposition splits a complex question into sub-questions upfront and answers them independently. IR-CoT interleaves retrieval with reasoning, one step at a time, so each step can use what the previous one retrieved.

items.title: Multi-query and RAG-Fusion
items.takeaway: Ambiguous user queries retrieve the wrong documents, so query translation has an LLM rewrite the question several ways. Multi-query merges the results, and RAG-Fusion ranks them with RRF.

items.title: Multi-representation, RAPTOR and ColBERT
items.takeaway: Advanced indexing changes *what* gets embedded: a keyword-rich summary instead of the raw chunk (multi-representation), a tree of recursive summaries (RAPTOR), or one embedding per token (ColBERT).

items.title: Routing and query construction
items.takeaway: Routing decides which data source should handle a query, and query construction splits the question into a semantic search term plus metadata filters that narrow the pool before similarity search.

items.title: Step-back prompting and HyDE
items.takeaway: Step-back retrieves with a more abstract version of the question alongside the original, and HyDE retrieves with a hypothetical answer document instead of the raw query.

items.title: Chunk sizing
items.takeaway: Size chunks in tokens, not characters, because embedding models enforce token limits, and choose the size and overlap to match the kind of content.

items.title: Chunking strategies
items.takeaway: Fixed-size chunking ignores structure. Recursive character splitting falls back through a hierarchy of separators, and sentence- or paragraph-aware splitting wins when units of meaning matter.

items.title: Why chunk, and overlap
items.takeaway: Whole documents can't be embedded well, because embedding models have input limits and long inputs blur into an averaged vector. Chunks trade retrieval precision against context, and overlap protects sentences that get cut at a boundary.

items.title: Deduplication
items.takeaway: Deduplicate before embedding, otherwise repeated content counts twice and skews retrieval. A hash catches exact copies, and shingling with MinHash catches near-duplicates.

items.title: Document metadata
items.takeaway: The Document object owns its metadata: it's a container for the clean text plus stable identifiers and attributes, captured once at ingestion when the information is still unambiguous.

items.title: Format-specific extraction
items.takeaway: Ingestion turns every file on disk into one consistent representation (clean text + metadata), and each file format needs its own extraction path because each one stores content differently.

items.title: Text cleaning
items.takeaway: Clean text has normalised whitespace, no page artifacts, its reading order intact and correct decoding. Garbage in, garbage out.

items.title: Context assembly
items.takeaway: Before generation, the retrieved chunks are reordered against lost-in-the-middle, trimmed to fit the token budget, deduplicated, and formatted with source labels and delimiters.

items.title: Grounding and failure modes
items.takeaway: A grounded prompt tells the model to answer only from labelled sources and to cite them, but RAG can still fail through ignored context, conflicting chunks, empty retrieval or injected instructions.

items.title: RAG evaluation
items.takeaway: Evaluate a RAG system in two halves, retrieval (did the right chunks come back?) and generation (is the answer grounded, relevant and complete?), against a golden Q&A set.

items.title: RAG pipeline modules
items.takeaway: A from-scratch RAG pipeline is eight modules, each with one responsibility, orchestrated into two public flows: `index()` and `query()`.

items.title: Bi-encoders vs cross-encoders
items.takeaway: Bi-encoders embed the query and the passage separately, which is cheap and good for searching everything. Cross-encoders read them together with full attention, which is expensive and precise. So retrieve with the first and rerank with the second.

items.title: Dense vs sparse embeddings
items.takeaway: Dense embeddings spread meaning across a few hundred uninterpretable dimensions, while sparse embeddings have one slot per vocabulary term. SPLADE learns a sparse vector with term expansion.

items.title: HNSW and IVF indexing
items.takeaway: Indexing organises the embedded chunks into a structure that makes similarity search fast. HNSW does it with a layered graph, and IVF does it with buckets of clusters it can skip.

items.title: Hybrid search and RRF
items.takeaway: Dense search misses exact identifiers and phrasing, so hybrid search adds sparse search too. Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges the two lists by rank, because their raw scores live on incompatible scales.

items.title: In-memory vector store
items.takeaway: Embed chunks in batches, keep the vectors in one contiguous normalised NumPy array with a parallel metadata list, and similarity search becomes a single vectorised operation.

items.title: MMR (Maximal Marginal Relevance)
items.takeaway: MMR picks results one at a time, rewarding relevance to the query and penalising similarity to what's already been picked, so the generator doesn't get the same fact five times.

items.title: Retriever design
items.takeaway: The vector store only returns the raw top-k. The retriever owns the query side: it embeds the query, applies metadata filters and a score threshold, and returns ranked SearchResults.

items.title: Top-k similarity search
items.takeaway: One matrix–vector product scores the query against every stored chunk, and `argpartition` finds the top k without sorting all n scores.

items.title: Vector database types
items.takeaway: A vector database stores data as vectors (direction and magnitude) in a multi-dimensional space. The main types differ in where the vectors live: memory, disk, a cluster, or a graph.

items.title: API styles overview
items.takeaway: Pick the API style for the job: SOAP for strict enterprise contracts, REST for resource-based web APIs, GraphQL to stop over/underfetching, gRPC for fast server-to-server calls, WebSockets for live two-way data, and webhooks for events.

items.title: gRPC
items.takeaway: gRPC is a remote-procedure-call framework for server-to-server traffic. It's fast because Protocol Buffers send compact binary instead of bloated JSON, and HTTP/2 multiplexes many calls over one TCP connection.

items.title: REST API
items.takeaway: REST is a client-server, stateless style for resource-based APIs, defined by five constraints: client-server, stateless, cacheable, layered and uniform interface.

items.title: SOAP
items.takeaway: SOAP is a strict, XML-only, W3C-standard protocol built around security and reliability. It exposes actions rather than resources and isn't tied to HTTP.

items.title: Idempotency
items.takeaway: An idempotent operation gives the same result whether it runs once or many times. It matters because retries happen, and a retried payment must not charge twice.

items.title: Monolith vs microservices
items.takeaway: A monolith ships as one unit on one shared DB, so ACID transactions are easy but scaling is all-or-nothing. Microservices split by business capability with private data and independent deploys, and need patterns like SAGA for consistency.

items.title: API authentication and token-based auth
items.takeaway: Authentication verifies who the client is so only authorized callers reach a resource. Token-based auth does that once, then hands back a token so the user doesn't re-enter credentials on every request.

items.title: Basic authentication
items.takeaway: Basic auth sends `username:password`, Base64-encoded, in a request header on every request. Base64 is just encoding, so it's only safe over TLS.

items.title: JWT authentication
items.takeaway: A JWT is a signed `header.payload.signature` token that carries the user's identity itself, so the server can verify requests without storing any session. In other words, it's stateless.

items.title: OAuth and SSO
items.takeaway: OAuth lets a third-party app act on a user's behalf with a short-lived, limited access token instead of the user's password. SSO (via OpenID or SAML) lets one login cover many apps.

items.title: Session authentication
items.takeaway: In session auth the server stores the login state and hands the client only a random session ID in a cookie. That makes revoking easy, but every server needs access to the session store.

items.title: Types of cache
items.takeaway: Where the cache lives sets the trade-off. Distributed caches shard keys across nodes, a global cache is one shared store, a CDN serves static files near users, and server-side vs client-side trades consistency for scale.

items.title: Caching basics
items.takeaway: A cache keeps copies of data in fast storage close to whoever asks, so repeat requests skip the slow source. The cost is having to evict and invalidate entries to stay small and correct.

items.title: Cache eviction policies
items.takeaway: When the cache is full, the eviction policy decides who leaves. Match it to the access pattern: LRU for "recent is likely again", MRU when you never want the same item twice, LFU when popularity matters.

items.title: Cache read strategies
items.takeaway: On a read, decide who talks to the DB. In cache-aside the app does (4 hops), in read-through the cache does (and collapses concurrent misses), and refresh-ahead reloads hot keys before their TTL runs out.

items.title: Cache write strategies
items.takeaway: On a write, choose where the data goes first. Write-through updates cache then DB (consistent, slower writes), write-around skips the cache (more read misses), and write-back updates the DB later and async (fast, risks losing data).

items.title: Database migrations
items.takeaway: A migration is a controlled change to a database. Schema migrations change its structure step by step, and data migrations move data from one DB to another.

items.title: Indexing vs sharding
items.takeaway: An index is an extra data structure that makes lookups on one table fast. Sharding splits a huge database into non-overlapping pieces across machines, which is horizontal scaling.

items.title: N+1 query problem
items.takeaway: N+1 means one query to fetch N parent rows, then N more queries for each one's children. The fix is to load the children together, with a JOIN (eager loading) or a batch fetch.

items.title: ORM (Object Relational Mapping)
items.takeaway: An ORM lets you work with the database through objects instead of raw SQL. That's convenient, but you pay in translation overhead, leaky abstraction and less control.

items.title: CI/CD
items.takeaway: CI builds and tests every push automatically so breakage shows up immediately. CD takes a passing build and packages it for staging/production: delivery when a human releases it, deployment when it goes out automatically.

items.title: Git basics
items.takeaway: Git is a distributed version control system: every developer has the full repo locally. Changes move from working directory → staging area → local repo → remote repo, while GitHub is just the cloud host for that remote.

items.title: TDD and what to test
items.takeaway: TDD is the red → green → refactor loop: write a failing test, make it pass with minimal code, then clean up while it stays green. Whatever the method, cover the happy path, edge cases, error handling and business-critical paths.

items.title: Testing pyramid
items.takeaway: Have many fast, cheap unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and a few slow, expensive end-to-end tests on top. Not testing costs more than testing.

items.title: Browser rendering
items.takeaway: The browser turns raw bytes into a DOM and a CSSOM, merges them into a render tree, computes layout, then paints. Scripts and CSS can block that pipeline.

items.title: DNS resolution
items.takeaway: DNS maps a domain name to an IP address. It checks local caches first, then walks root → TLD → authoritative name server only if nothing local knows the answer.

items.title: HTTP basics
items.takeaway: HTTP is the stateless request/response protocol web clients and servers talk over. HTTPS is the same thing with everything encrypted by SSL/TLS.

items.title: HTTP status codes
items.takeaway: A status code's first digit says who is responsible: 1xx info, 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client's fault, 5xx server's fault.

items.title: Web servers (Apache vs NGINX)
items.takeaway: A web server listens on a port and answers requests with the resource asked for. Apache uses a thread per connection, while NGINX is event-driven and async, which is why it copes better with high traffic.

items.title: Feature engineering steps
items.takeaway: Feature engineering turns raw data into useful data: EDA, then missing values, class imbalance, outliers, and finally scaling (normalisation or standardisation).

items.title: AdaBoost
items.takeaway: AdaBoost chains decision stumps, gives each one a vote weighted by how well it did, and boosts the weights of misclassified rows so the next stump concentrates on them.

items.title: Bagging vs boosting
items.takeaway: Bagging trains models in parallel on random subsets and votes or averages to cut variance, while boosting trains weak learners in sequence so each one fixes the previous one's errors.

items.title: Gradient boosting (regression)
items.takeaway: Gradient boosting starts from the mean prediction, then keeps adding small trees that predict the remaining residuals, each scaled down by a learning rate.

items.title: Random forest: filling missing data
items.takeaway: A random forest fills missing values by starting with a simple guess, then refining it with a proximity matrix that weights similar samples, and repeating until the values stop changing.

items.title: Random forest
items.takeaway: A random forest trains many decision trees, each on a bootstrapped sample and a random subset of features, and takes a majority vote so that each tree's overfitting averages out.

items.title: XGBoost
items.takeaway: XGBoost builds trees in sequence on the residuals and picks splits by similarity score and gain, with a λ regulariser in the denominator.

items.title: AI vs ML vs DL vs DS
items.takeaway: DL sits inside ML, which sits inside AI, and data science draws on all of them along with statistics.

items.title: Bias–variance tradeoff
items.takeaway: Aim for a model with low bias and low variance: it fits the true pattern and stays stable across different data splits.

items.title: Supervised vs unsupervised learning
items.takeaway: Supervised learning trains on labelled data to predict a dependent feature, while unsupervised learning has no dependent feature and finds hidden structure on its own.

items.title: Classification metrics
items.takeaway: Precision cares about false positives, recall cares about false negatives, and the F-β score blends the two with β choosing which one matters more.

items.title: Decision tree splits: entropy, Gini, information gain
items.takeaway: A decision tree picks, at each node, the feature whose split gives the highest information gain, meaning the biggest drop in impurity.

items.title: Gradient descent
items.takeaway: Gradient descent repeatedly steps each parameter against the slope of the cost function, scaled by a learning rate α, until it converges at the minimum.

items.title: K-nearest neighbours (KNN)
items.takeaway: KNN predicts from the k closest training points: a majority vote for classification, an average for regression.

items.title: Linear regression
items.takeaway: Linear regression fits the straight line h(x) = θ₀ + θ₁x that minimises the squared error between predicted and actual values.

items.title: Logistic regression
items.takeaway: Logistic regression is linear regression squashed through a sigmoid into a probability between 0 and 1, trained with log loss so the cost stays convex.

items.title: R² and adjusted R²
items.takeaway: R² measures how much better a regression fits than just predicting the mean, and adjusted R² penalises predictors that don't earn their place.

items.title: Ridge and Lasso regression
items.takeaway: Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) add a slope penalty to the cost function to stop overfitting, and Lasso can also drop useless features entirely.

items.title: ROC–AUC
items.takeaway: The ROC curve plots TPR against FPR across every threshold, and the area under it (AUC) lets you compare classifiers with a single number.

items.title: Support vector machines (SVM)
items.takeaway: An SVM classifies by finding the hyperplane w·x + b = 0 that separates the classes with the widest possible margin.

items.title: K-means and the elbow method
items.takeaway: K-means groups unlabelled data around k centroids, alternating between assigning points and moving centroids, and the elbow method picks k where WCSS stops dropping sharply.

items.title: One-hot encoding and bag of words
items.takeaway: One-hot turns each word into a sparse binary vector, and bag of words turns a whole sentence into a vector of word counts. Both ignore word order and meaning.

items.title: Stemming vs lemmatization
items.takeaway: Stemming chops affixes off to reach a crude root that may not be a real word, while lemmatization maps each word to its dictionary form (the lemma) using its part of speech.

items.title: TF-IDF
items.takeaway: TF-IDF scores a word by how often it appears in a sentence, weighted down by how many sentences contain it, so words found everywhere score zero.

items.title: Tokenization and stop words
items.takeaway: Tokenization breaks text into tokens, and stop-word removal throws away the common words that carry almost no meaning before any further processing.

items.title: Word embeddings and Word2Vec
items.takeaway: Word embeddings are dense real-valued vectors where words with similar meanings sit close together, and Word2Vec learns them with a small neural network using CBOW or skip-gram.

items.title: Recommender system types
items.takeaway: Collaborative filtering recommends what similar users liked, content-based filtering recommends items similar to the ones you already like, and hybrid systems combine the two to cover each one's weak spots.

items.title: Central tendency and dispersion
items.takeaway: Mean, median and mode tell you where the data sits, and range, IQR, variance and SD tell you how spread out it is. With outliers, prefer median and IQR.

items.title: Covariance vs correlation
items.takeaway: Covariance tells you only the direction two variables move together, while correlation scales it to the range −1 to +1 so you also get the strength.

items.title: Percentiles, the five-number summary and outlier detection
items.takeaway: To flag outliers, use IQR fences (Q1 − 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR) on skewed data and |z| > 3 on normal data, so check the shape of the distribution before picking a method.

items.title: Skewness and kurtosis
items.takeaway: Skewness measures how lopsided a distribution is, which shows up as the gap between mean and median, and kurtosis measures how heavy its tails are compared with its centre.

items.title: Types of data and types of statistics
items.takeaway: Descriptive statistics summarise the data you have and inferential statistics generalise from a sample to a population, while data itself is either categorical (nominal or ordinal) or numerical (discrete or continuous).

items.title: Chi-square test
items.takeaway: The chi-square test checks claims about population proportions in categorical data by comparing observed counts with expected counts.

items.title: Confidence intervals, z-test and t-test
items.takeaway: A confidence interval is the point estimate ± a margin of error. Use z when the population SD is known and t (with df = n − 1) when it isn't.

items.title: Hypothesis testing
items.takeaway: A hypothesis test assumes the null (no effect) and asks whether the experimental data is extreme enough, in one tail or both, to reject it.

items.title: P-value, significance and Type I/II errors
items.takeaway: If p ≤ 0.05, reject H₀. A Type I error rejects a true H₀ (a false positive), and a Type II error keeps a false H₀ (a false negative).

items.title: Sampling methods
items.takeaway: In probability sampling every member has an equal, random chance of being picked. Non-probability sampling picks by judgement or convenience, which is easier but biased.

items.title: Central limit theorem (CLT)
items.takeaway: As sample size grows, the distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution, whatever shape the original data has.

items.title: Common distributions: uniform, normal, Bernoulli
items.takeaway: In a normal distribution 68%, 95% and 99.7% of the data falls within 1, 2 and 3 SDs of the mean. Uniform gives every outcome equal odds, and Bernoulli has only the outcomes 0 and 1.

items.title: Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
items.takeaway: Bayes' theorem turns P(B|A) into P(A|B) by weighting it with the prior P(A) and dividing by the marginal P(B).

items.title: Permutations and combinations
items.takeaway: Use a permutation when order matters (nPr = n!/(n−r)!) and a combination when it doesn't (nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!)).

items.title: Probability basics and the addition rule
items.takeaway: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), and the overlap term drops out only when A and B are mutually exclusive.

items.title: Z-score and the standard normal distribution
items.takeaway: A z-score gives how many standard deviations a point lies from the mean, and z-scoring normal data produces the standard normal distribution, with μ = 0 and σ = 1.
